1:
Two days after the feast of tabernacles had closed, the congregation gathered again in a wholly different key, and the witnesses first fix the calendar and then the meaning of the mourning. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the crowded month: the feast of trumpets fell on the first day, the feast of tabernacles began on the fourteenth and ran seven days to the twenty-second, on the twenty-third the people separated from their foreign wives and children, and on this twenty-fourth they kept a solemn fast of confession and reading of the law, which they closed by renewing their covenant. John Wesley explains why the grief comes only now: during the festival their consciences had been awakened and their hearts filled with sorrow for sin, but they were not suffered to vent it in that time of public joy; now they resume those thoughts and set apart a day for humiliation.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the outward marks of the day. The people assembled with fasting, with sackcloth — the penitential garments of hair he notes at Joel 1:8 — and with earth spread upon their heads, the tokens of deep mourning seen in 1 Samuel 4:12, 2 Samuel 1:2, and Job 2:12. Charles Ellicott adds that after one day of rest the people came together with every sign of sorrow, even to dust on the head, so that here the external signs and the internal spirit were one.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the whole as the fast that God has chosen. It was a day to afflict the soul, after Isaiah 58:5, and a day to loose the bands of wickedness, which is the fast God chose in Isaiah 58:6; without that loosing, he warns, spreading sackcloth and ashes under us is but a jest. They had been restrained from weeping at the feast, in Nehemiah 8:9, but now they were directed to weep, for the joy of holy feasts must give way to the sorrow of solemn fasts. Above all it was a day of communion with God: they fasted to him, even to him, after Zechariah 7:5, both speaking to him in prayer and hearing him speak by his word — for fasting without prayer, Henry says, is a body without a soul, a worthless carcase. The reformed John Gill simply anchors the date in the seventh month, Tisri, two days after the feast was ended. The witnesses converge: the calendar is exact, but the point is the heart.
2:
The seed of Israel separated themselves from all strangers, and the witnesses divide over precisely what that separation was. The reformed John Gill takes it of the mixed marriages: genuine Israelites who had married Gentile wives, whether before Ezra's reformation and undiscovered, or since, were now convinced upon the reading of the law and put away those wives, which he calls a proof of the truth of their repentance. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it the same way, of an unnecessary society with the heathen and particularly of the strange women some had married; for though Ezra had done this before, there were either new delinquents or old ones undiscovered, who now showed their repentance by forsaking their beloved sins and dearest relations. Adam Clarke likewise recalls that the reformation had begun under Ezra, at Ezra 10:3, but that either more were found out or some had taken back the wives they had put away.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch resist that narrowing. This separation, they insist, does not specially relate to the dissolution of the marriages contracted with heathen women, nor to any measure taken that only Israelites should be admitted to the assembly; it was rather a voluntary renunciation of all connection with the heathen and of heathen customs. Charles Ellicott hears in the very word a deep propriety — the change to "seed" marks a people who carefully avoided the many aliens among them throughout this fast — and he notes that these opening verses give only the programme of what is afterward filled up, so that the very praise for which they stood was itself filled with confession.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers both the act and its lesson. Because they were a holy seed, appropriated to God and more excellent than their neighbours, they separated themselves from all the strangers with whom they had mingled and joined in affinity; Ezra had parted them from their strange wives years before, but they had relapsed, and now they separated from the strange children as well as the strange wives. Those who intend by prayers and covenants to join themselves to God, Henry urges, must first separate themselves from sin and sinners, for what communion hath light with darkness, after 2 Corinthians 6:14. And with the separation went the confession: they stood and owned not only their own sins but the iniquities of their fathers, acknowledging, as Clarke observes, that they had copied their fathers' offences with that very example before their eyes. The witnesses agree on the penitence, and differ only on how wide the renunciation reached.
3:
The day fell into ordered halves of word and worship, and the witnesses attend both to the posture and to the arithmetic of the hours. The reformed John Gill sets the people standing in their place in the outer court, where men used to stand to pray and confess, reading in the book of the law that they might the better know the mind and will of God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch parse the two portions: they remained standing in their place, as at Nehemiah 8:7, and listened to the reading of the law a fourth part of the day, about three hours, and for another fourth part they confessed their sins and worshipped the LORD their God — a confession and worship then more fully described through the verses that follow. Charles Ellicott adds that both day and night were divided into four parts, all orders standing in their respective places, the reading occupying the morning and the worship the afternoon; and he notes that it is now the worship that is made prominent, as the reading had been prominent in the chapter before.

Over the shape of the whole day the witnesses vary. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reckons three hours for reading and three for confessing and praying, so that they stayed together six hours and spent all that time in the solemn acts of religion, the varying of the exercises making it the less tedious; yet he records that Bishop Patrick thought they spent the whole twelve hours of the day in devotion, reading from six to nine, praying from nine to twelve, reading again from twelve to three, and praying from three to six. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers just such a fuller scheme from Calmet: they began at the first hour and continued to the third, then from the third to the sixth, from the sixth to the ninth, and from the ninth to the twelfth — hearing the law read standing, prostrating themselves in confession, and rising to praise God for his mercy. John Wesley keeps to the plain measure of three hours to a quarter, in a day of twelve hours, probably from the morning sacrifice to the evening.

The witnesses do not contend over the substance, only over the count: whether the sacred exercises filled two quarters of the day or the whole of it. What they agree upon is the wisdom of the pairing. The word read would furnish matter for prayer, Henry observes, and prayer would make the word the more profitable; for in the glass of the law they might see their own deformities and know what to acknowledge and what to amend. The work of a fast-day is good work, and, as both Henry and Wesley say in nearly the same breath, we should endeavour to make a day's work, a good day's work, of it.
4:
Eight Levites mount the platform and cry aloud, and the witnesses weigh the scene, the scaffold, and the puzzle of the names. The reformed John Gill sets them upon an elevated place, the stairs where the Levites stood at the time of sacrifice, that they might be seen and heard by the people. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch call it the scaffold of the Levites, the platform erected for them as at Nehemiah 8:4, and observe that the repetition of their names in the next verse shows two distinct acts: the Levites first cried to God, addressing to him their confessions and supplications, and then called upon the assembled congregation to worship. Eight names are given in each list, five of them identical, and the difference of the other three the witnesses cannot fully resolve. Charles Ellicott reads "the scaffold of the Levites" without the comma, taking it for the steps of ascent to Ezra's pulpit of Nehemiah 8:2; he guesses Bani and Chenani to be the Binnui and Haman of Nehemiah 10:9, and he marks a telling detail — the Levites cried to "their God," whereas when the people are addressed it is "your God," so that these eight first offered a prayer of their own which the record does not insert.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley pictures the ministers spread over several pulpits, each teaching, praying, or blessing God with the portion of the congregation allotted him; and he reads the loud voice as the token of their deep sense of sin and misery and their earnest, importunate desire of God's mercy.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the manner and the wisdom of it. The ministers are twice named, and either they prayed successively, after the apostle's rule that you may all prophesy one by one in 1 Corinthians 14:31, or there were eight several congregations each with a Levite to preside. They cried with a loud voice, Henry insists, not that God might the better hear them, as Baal's worshippers imagined of their god, but that the people might hear, and to excite their fervency. And the double work of the day was prayer and praise together: for the work of praise is not unseasonable on a fast-day, since in all acts of devotion we must aim to give unto God the glory due to his name. The summary of their prayers stands here on record, Henry adds, though much more was no doubt said, else the confessing and worshipping would not have filled a fourth part of the day, much less two. The witnesses converge on a picture of ordered, fervent, public devotion, in which the Levites lead and the whole people answer.
5:
The Levites summon the people to their feet with a doxology, and the witnesses attend to the call, the posture, and the disputed authorship. The reformed John Gill reads the roll of names plainly — then the Levites, even Jeshua and the rest. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the burden of the summons: "Stand up and bless the LORD your God for ever and ever; and blessed be the name of thy glory, which is exalted above all blessing and praise" — the theme of the whole confession, which the succeeding verses will unfold from the creation to the exile. Charles Ellicott studies the wording closely. Hashabniah among these names is found nowhere else; no reason is given why this company differs somewhat from the former, and the Septuagint arbitrarily omits every name after Kadmiel while inserting "and Ezra said" before the next verse — so that the psalm, he suggests, was perhaps composed by Ezra but uttered by the Levites in the name of the congregation. The three phrases of the opening, he notes, mark how the address to the people glides into direct adoration of God; and the striking phrase "thy glorious name" is found again, literally, only in Psalms 72:19.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on the posture as a rebuke to careless worshippers. It is the shameless custom of many congregations, he complains, to sit still while they profess to bless and praise God in psalm and hymn; and he asks whether such persons ever felt the spirit of devotion so employed, since by the mere prevalence of habit they have counteracted an attitude most friendly to the acts of worship. Standing up to bless is no small thing, but the fitting bodily confession of the soul that adores.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the words the very heart of praise. The congregation is called upon to signify their concurrence by standing up, and so the minister directs himself to God, "Blessed be thy glorious name." That name, Henry observes, is exalted above all blessing and praise: it needs not the praises of the creatures, nor is any addition made to its glory by them, for the best performances even of the angels fall infinitely short of what it deserves. Put all the praises of heaven and earth together, and not the thousandth part is said of what should be said of the glory of God; our goodness extendeth not to him. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the names, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott the wording and its possible Ezran hand, Clarke the reverent posture, and Henry the truth that the God so blessed is infinitely above every blessing his people can bring — which is itself the ground of their bold confession in the verses to come.
6:
The confession begins where all true confession begins, with the God who is God alone, and the witnesses trace the ascent from creation to worship. The reformed John Gill fixes the first clause on the divine name: thou, even thou, art LORD alone, whose name alone is Jehovah, the one only true and living God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch expound the sweep of the sentence. Jahve alone is God, the maker of heaven and earth and of every creature in them; and to exalt his almightiness the notion of heaven is heightened by "the heaven of heavens," as in Deuteronomy 10:14 and 1 Kings 8:27, and that of earth by "the sea and all therein," after Psalms 146:6; the host in view, drawn from Genesis 2:1, is here the host of heaven, which worships him.

Over the clause "thou preservest them all" the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers on the Hebrew, which he renders "thou givest life to them all," and on the host of heaven that prostrates itself before God. How near this comes, he muses, to Kepler's fancy that all the heavenly bodies are instinct with life and navigate the great expanse on wings fitted to their orbits; yet he draws back, for to preserve in life or in being is a very good meaning that does not necessarily imply vitality, since we call a tree alive while it flourishes and dead when it withers. Charles Ellicott keeps to the plainer sense: this comprehensive preserving of all things is reproduced only at Hebrews 1:3, where the Son upholds all things by the word of his power; and the "host of heaven" that worships, though it may first mean the stars, is here the angels, as in Psalms 103:21.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into an act of adoration. God is here owned as the only living and true God, self-existent and independent, so that there is no God besides him; as the Creator of all things, for the first article of our creed is fitly made the first article of our praises; as the great Protector of the whole creation, whose providence reaches to the highest beings, for they need it, and to the meanest, for they are not slighted by it; and as the object of the creatures' praises, since the world of holy angels worships him, and yet his name is exalted above all their blessing. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the incommunicable name, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott the Creator who upholds and the hosts who adore, Clarke the reach of the preserving hand, and Henry the truth that the God whom Israel now implores is the fountain of all beings, so that a people undone may yet appeal to the maker and keeper of all.
7:
From the Creator the prayer turns to the covenant, and the witnesses rehearse the free grace shown to Abram. The reformed John Gill marks the sovereignty of the choice: God chose Abram from among the Chaldeans and out of his father's family, calling him where he had no claim. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence forward — thou art Jahve, the God who didst choose Abram and broughtest him forth out of Ur of the Chaldees and gavest him the name of Abraham — reading it as the opening of that long recital of grace which will run from the call of the patriarch to the gift of the land. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke points, for the choosing of Abram and the bringing out of Ur, to the pillar and the guidance of Exodus 13:21, and for the meaning of the new name to the covenant of Genesis 17:5, where Abram becomes Abraham, the father of a multitude.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out what these bare clauses carry. God's favour to Abraham was distinguishing — "thou didst choose him" — and his grace in him was powerful to bring him out of Ur of the Chaldees; and in giving him the name of Abraham he put honour upon him as his own and assured him that he should be the father of many nations. Look unto Abraham your father, Henry urges with the prophet of Isaiah 51:2, and see free grace glorified in him; for the calling of the one man from an idolatrous stock is the first great instance of that mercy the whole prayer will magnify.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very structure of the verse teaches them. It begins, as Keil and Delitzsch observe, by naming God again — "thou art the LORD the God" — so that the choice of Abram is grounded not in any worth of the man but in the will of the God who is Creator and Jehovah alone. The bringing forth out of Ur is an act of pure deliverance, a plucking of one soul out of the darkness of Chaldean idolatry; and the giving of the new name is the seal of a new destiny, the pledge that from this called and renamed man a nation and a promise should come. What the confessing people find here is the taproot of their own existence: they stand before God as the seed of the man he chose, and if grace made Abraham what he was, then grace, and not their own deserving, is the only ground on which his children can now plead. The recital of favour begins, fittingly, with the sovereign call that made a people out of nothing.
8:
The covenant with Abraham is the hinge of the whole recital, and the witnesses dwell on the faithful heart and the faithful God. The reformed John Gill glosses "foundest his heart faithful before thee" of a true believer in God's word and promises, closely attached to the fear of him and the keeping of his commands, as appeared most of all in the trial of him when he offered up his son in Genesis 22:2. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the substance of the covenant: God made it with Abraham to give the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Jebusites, and the Girgashites to his seed, and hast performed thy word, for thou art righteous — a righteousness, they note, that is precisely God's fidelity to his own promise, the same word owned again at Nehemiah 9:33 and grounded in Deuteronomy 32:4. Charles Ellicott adds only the small observing note that the Hivites, elsewhere named among the nations, are here for some reason omitted from the list.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a lesson in the very nature of covenant grace. The covenant God made with Abraham was to give the land of Canaan to him and his seed — a land which was itself a type of the better country — and this covenant was sure, for God found Abraham's heart faithful before him. Yet Henry will not let that faithfulness be read as the ground of the promise rather than its fruit: God found Abraham's heart faithful, he says, because he made it so, for faith is not of ourselves but is the gift of God; and having made the heart faithful, he performed his words. With the upright he will show himself upright, after Psalms 18:25, and wherever he finds a faithful heart he will be found a faithful God.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they hold two truths in one clause. On the one side stands Abraham's fidelity, proved to the uttermost when he did not withhold his only son; on the other stands God's fidelity, which gave the land exactly as he had sworn and which the confessing people now plead as their only hope. The land is named by its old inhabitants, the six or seven doomed nations, precisely to show how large a word God had bound himself to keep, and how fully he kept it. For a congregation that has just owned its own unfaithfulness, the point is pastoral as well as historical: the covenant did not stand or fall by Israel's constancy but by the righteousness of God, who performs his word because he is just. If grace made Abraham faithful and justice made God keep faith, then the seed of Abraham, however faithless, may still appeal to a covenant that rests on God and not on them.
9:
The prayer descends from the patriarch to his enslaved children, and the witnesses mark the God who sees and hears. The reformed John Gill will not let "didst see the affliction of our fathers in Egypt" be read of a bare spectator: God looked upon them in the hard bondage that made their lives bitter with pity and compassion, and looked in order to act, sending them a deliverer. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the two things compressed into the single verse and unfolded in the two that follow: the affliction of the Israelites in Egypt, which God saw, after the language of Exodus 3:7, and out of which he delivered them by the signs and wonders shown upon Pharaoh; and the crying for help at the Red Sea, when the people perceived Pharaoh with his horsemen and chariots in pursuit, at Exodus 14:10, and God gave them help by dividing the waters.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the remembrance as deeply seasonable to the moment of prayer. It was fitting to recall the deliverance out of Egypt now that they were interceding for the perfecting of their deliverance out of Babylon; for they had then been delivered in compassion to their affliction, in answer to their cry, and in resistance of the pride and insolence of their persecutors. God saw the affliction and heard the cry: these are the two motions of divine mercy that the whole exodus will magnify, and they are exactly what a bondaged people, restored but not yet free, most needs to plead.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse teaches by its very order. First God sees, then God hears — the affliction in Egypt and the cry at the sea — and both are answered not by anything in Israel but by the covenant just named, the word God swore to Abraham and performs because he is righteous. Gill presses the tenderness of the seeing, that it was no idle observation but the look that stoops to save; Keil and Delitzsch press the historical shape, that the seeing issues in the plagues and the hearing in the dividing of the sea; Henry presses the encouragement, that a God who once saw and heard is the same God still, so that the fathers' experience becomes the children's argument. The confessing congregation, rehearsing how their God bent low over a suffering people and would not turn away from their cry, lay the ground for their own petition: the God who saw Egypt and heard the sea has not grown deaf or blind, and the affliction now upon them is not hidden from his eyes.
10:
The plagues and the drowning are recalled as the shape of God's answer, and the witnesses read them as at once judgment on Pharaoh and glory to God. The reformed John Gill takes the signs and wonders shown upon Pharaoh, his servants, and all the people of his land to be the inflicting of the ten plagues, the whole apparatus of the Egyptian ruin. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, whose words lean on Deuteronomy 6:22, fix the reason the text itself assigns: God wrought these signs because he knew that the Egyptians dealt proudly against Israel, and so he made himself a name, as it is this day. The pride of the oppressor is the occasion, and the vindication of God's name the end; the two are bound together, so that the humbling of Pharaoh is the exalting of the LORD.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses that very point. The deliverance out of Egypt was wrought in resistance of the pride and insolence of their persecutors; wherein they dealt proudly, God showed himself above them, after the confession of Jethro in Exodus 18:11, and so he got himself a name, for he had said, "I will get me honour upon Pharaoh," in Exodus 14:17. Even to this day, Henry adds, the name of God is glorified for that wonderful work; the signs and wonders were the means, and the destruction of the enemy the visible proof, that no proud power can stand against the God of Israel.

The witnesses do not divide, and the logic they draw out is one the confessing people needed. God's proceedings against Egypt were not arbitrary displays but the just answer to an arrogance that had ground his people down; the same haughtiness that oppressed the weak provoked the strong hand of heaven. And the outcome was a name — a reputation for delivering power that ran through all the generations and that the Levites now invoke, "as it is this day." For a congregation still under the heel of foreign kings, the memory is pointed: the God who broke the proudest empire of the ancient world for the sake of his afflicted people, and made his own name great in the breaking, has lost neither his power nor his hatred of the oppressor. The plagues are recalled not as a closed chapter of history but as a standing pledge of what the LORD is, and of what he may yet do for the seed he redeemed.
11:
The dividing of the sea is remembered as the crown of the exodus, and the witnesses catch both the miracle and the poetry that first sang it. The reformed John Gill reads the plain wonder: God divided the sea before the Israelites, so that they went through the midst of it on dry land, a path opened where there had been no path. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the deliverance in its narrative frame — the crying at the Red Sea answered by the parting of the waters, the people passing over and their pursuers cast into the deeps — while Charles Ellicott turns to the phrase "as a stone into the mighty waters" and bids the reader compare the Song of Moses in Exodus 15:5, marking in the Hebrew both the identity of the image and its variation, so that the Levites' prayer is heard consciously echoing the ancient triumph-hymn.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the double stroke of the one act. The deliverance of Israel was at the same time the destruction of their enemies: the people were led through, and their persecutors were thrown into the deeps as irrecoverably as a stone into the mighty waters. It was done miraculously, Henry observes, for signs and wonders were shown for the effecting of it; and the sea that was a wall of safety to the redeemed was a grave to the pursuer. The very element that opened to save closed to slay.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they let the verse do its appointed work in the confession. The parting of the sea is the great pattern of salvation in the Old Testament — a helpless people hemmed between the water and the sword, delivered by no strength of their own but by the bare hand of God, who makes a road through the deep and buries the oppressor in it. That the Levites reach for the words of Moses' song, as Ellicott shows, is itself significant: they are not inventing a new plea but standing in the oldest confession of Israel, that the LORD is a man of war who triumphs gloriously. For a congregation that has just owned its bondage to foreign kings, the memory carries a quiet hope. The God who cast Pharaoh's host into the sea like a stone is the God they now address; and if once he made the mighty waters the tomb of the proud and the highway of the redeemed, then the people he brought through the sea may still look to him to bring them through.
12:
The pillar of cloud and fire is remembered as the sign of God's abiding presence, and the witnesses dwell on its guidance and its grace. The reformed John Gill reads the day-pillar as a shelter for the Israelites from the heat of the sun in a dry and barren wilderness, a canopy over a marching people. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke opens the fuller meaning, for he distinguishes three offices the one miraculous cloud discharged: as a pillar it went before them in their journeys to point out their way; as a pillar of fire it stood with them through the night to give them light and to be a rallying-point for the whole camp; and as an extended cloud it hovered over them in their encampments, to refresh them with its dews and to screen them from the ardours of the sun. The same token of the divine presence guided, illuminated, and sheltered by turns.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep to the plain office named in the verse — thou leddest them in the day by a cloudy pillar and in the night by a pillar of fire, to give them light in the way wherein they should go — reading it as the next stage of that recital of favour which runs from the sea to Sinai. The pillar is God's own leading, the visible pledge that he who had brought them through the water would not leave them to lose their way in the waste.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the wonder of it. The pillar showed them which way they should go, when they should remove, and when and where they should rest; it directed all their stages and all their steps, and was besides a visible token of God's presence with them, to guide and to guard. And Henry marks that the Levites will name it again further on: though the people by their sins provoked God to withdraw and leave them to perish in the by-paths of the wilderness, yet in his manifold mercy he continued to lead them and took not away the pillar, as the prayer confesses at Nehemiah 9:19. When mercies, though forfeited, are still continued, Henry urges, we are bound to be doubly thankful. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the shade, Clarke the threefold service, Keil and Delitzsch the leading, and Henry the perseverance of a grace that guided a people who did not deserve to be guided — the constant fire and cloud over an inconstant camp.
13:
The confession reaches Sinai, and the witnesses honour both the descent of the Lawgiver and the goodness of the law. The reformed John Gill reads "thou camest down also upon mount Sinai" of the visible tokens of God's presence — the cloud, the fire, the smoke — which must of course be understood consistently with his omnipresence, for the God who fills heaven and earth stooped to a mountain. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the recital on: God came down upon Sinai and spake with them from heaven, and gave them right judgments and true laws, good statutes and commandments — the same fourfold gift then extended, in the verse following, to the sabbath and to all that was commanded by the hand of Moses. Charles Ellicott hears in "right judgments, true laws, good statutes" five of the very names given to God's law in the great acrostic of Psalms 119:1, applied first to the Sinaitic legislation and then to the later Mosaic ordinances; and he lays the emphasis on the adjectives — right, true, good — as belonging above all to the eternal principles of the Decalogue.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses that goodness through every part of the law. The moral and judicial precepts, he says, were all founded on natural equity; and even the ceremonial statutes were tokens of God's goodness, being types of gospel grace — so that nothing given at Sinai was arbitrary or unkind, but all bore the marks of the giver.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry counts the giving of the law the greatest favour of all that was done them and the greatest honour put upon them. The Lawgiver was very glorious: "thou didst not only send, but camest down thyself, and didst speak with them," after the wonder of Deuteronomy 4:33; and the law given was very good, for no nation under the sun had such right judgments, true laws, and good statutes, as Moses boasts in Deuteronomy 4:8. The moral and judicial precepts, Henry agrees with Wesley, were founded upon natural equity and the eternal reasons of good and evil, and even the ceremonial institutions were tokens of God's goodness and types of gospel grace. The witnesses do not divide. Gill guards the condescension of the descent, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott the fourfold excellence of the law, and Wesley and Henry its goodness in every part — so that the confessing people, who will presently own how grievously they broke this law, first acknowledge how good the law was that they broke, and how gracious the God who came down to give it.
14:
Among the gifts of Sinai the sabbath is singled out, and the witnesses weigh its privilege and its place. The reformed John Gill reads "madest known unto them thy holy sabbath" of a rest peculiar to the Jewish nation, a privilege granted them of rest both corporeal and spiritual, and typical of the rest that is in Christ. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in the word "madest known" a hint that they had let the ordinance slip: they appear to have forgotten this first of God's commandments during their long sojourning in Egypt, so that at Sinai it had in a manner to be revealed to them afresh. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott bids us note every word, and the prominence given to the sabbath among the other commandments, as illustrating how weighty this ordinance is throughout the book — the very thing that will be pressed in the sworn covenant of the chapter following, at Nehemiah 10:31.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the sabbath in the frame of the whole Sinai-gift. Particular notice is taken of the fourth commandment as a great favour, he observes: "thou madest known unto them thy holy sabbath," which was a token of God's special favour to them, distinguishing them from the nations who had revolted from God and quite lost that ancient part of revealed religion, and was likewise a means of keeping up their communion with him. With the law and the sabbath, Henry adds, God gave his good Spirit to instruct them, as the prayer will confess further on; and besides the law given on the mount, the five books of Moses, written as he was moved by the Holy Ghost, were constant instructions to them.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they let the verse carry its double weight of gift and obligation. The sabbath was a favour — a rest for the body, a type of the soul's rest, a badge of separation from the idolatrous nations, and a standing means of fellowship with God — and precisely because it was so great a favour, its neglect would prove so great a sin. Clarke's remark, that Egypt had all but effaced it, and Ellicott's, that the book will make the keeping of it a chief article of the renewed covenant, together frame the point: the people who now bless God for making his holy day known will presently bind themselves, under oath, to profane it no more. The rest that God gave in mercy, and made known where it had been forgotten, becomes in the confession both a benefit to be thankful for and a trust to be kept; and the God who commanded these precepts by the hand of Moses his servant is owned as gracious in the very law his people had so long broken.
15:
The wilderness provision is recalled — bread from heaven, water from the rock, and the promise of the land — and the witnesses mark each mercy. The reformed John Gill reads "gavest them bread from heaven for their hunger" simply of the manna, the food rained down to satisfy a starving people. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the three gifts together: bread from heaven for their hunger, water brought forth out of the rock for their thirst, and the sworn promise that they should go in to possess the land — the fulfilment of the word once given to Abraham, now carried through the desert toward Canaan. Charles Ellicott hears in "bread from heaven" a phrase our Lord consecrated for ever, when he took up the manna of the fathers and made it the figure of himself, the true bread from heaven, in John 6:32.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the plentiful care of it. God made provision for them in the wilderness that they might not perish for hunger: "thou gavest them bread from heaven, and water out of the rock," and, to hold up their hearts, a promise that they should go in and possess the land of Canaan. They had meat and drink, food convenient for the way, and the good land at their journey's end — what would they more? The daily bread and the sworn inheritance answered every need, both for the road and for the rest to which it led; and this same provision, Henry notes, the prayer will presently repeat as continued through forty years, notwithstanding all their provocations.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers the whole tenderness of the desert years into three gifts. There was bread where no field grew, water where the rock was dry, and a promise to carry a homeless people toward a home — mercy for the present hunger and hope for the future possession, held out together. Gill fixes the manna, Keil and Delitzsch the ordered supply of bread, water, and land, and Ellicott the deeper glory the gift would one day bear, when the manna became the type of Christ. For the confessing congregation, restored to the land but still straitened and afraid, the memory is an argument: the God who fed the fathers from heaven and drew them water from the flint, and swore to bring them in, is the God they now implore; and the bread and the water and the oath all say the same thing, that he does not lead his people out only to let them famish, but sustains them all the way to the inheritance he has promised.
16:
At the height of the recited mercies the confession breaks into its first great "but," and the witnesses feel the force of the contrast. The reformed John Gill reads "they and our fathers dealt proudly" of a people who behaved in a haughty manner toward God their kind benefactor — the very hand that fed them repaid with insolence. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the grammar that drives the point home: the pronoun "they" is emphatic and thrown to the front, set in deliberate contrast to all the benefits just named, and the contrast is heightened by the phrase "even our fathers," which they defend against those who would strike it out. Words are heaped up to describe the stiff-necked resistance of the people — they dealt proudly, they hardened their necks, they hearkened not — and the hardening of the neck, an image from Exodus 32:9 and Exodus 33:3, already glances forward to the golden calf. Charles Ellicott adds the sharp irony that the same word "dealt proudly" was used of the Egyptians themselves in Exodus 18:11: the redeemed had learned the arrogance of their oppressors.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry probes the root of the rebellion. Pride, he says, is at the bottom of men's obstinacy and disobedience; they think it below them to bow their necks to God's yoke and count it a piece of state to set up their own will against the will of God himself. And he names two things they failed to heed, which, had they weighed them, would have kept them from such folly: the word of God they heard, but they did not hearken to his commandments; and the works of God they saw, but they were not mindful of his wonders. Had they duly considered those wonders as miracles, Henry reasons, they would have obeyed from a principle of faith and holy fear; had they considered them as mercies, they would have obeyed from a principle of gratitude and holy love.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse turns the whole prayer upon its hinge. Everything before was gift — the call of Abraham, the exodus, the pillar, the law, the manna; and now, against all of it, stands the ingratitude of the fathers, who took the mercies and hardened their hearts. Gill fixes the haughtiness, Keil and Delitzsch the emphatic contrast and its backward reach to Sinai, Ellicott the bitter likeness to Egypt, and Henry the pride that lies beneath all disobedience. The confessing congregation names the sin not to excuse it but to feel its weight, for they are the children of these fathers, and the same proud neck that would not bow at Sinai is the neck they now bring, at last, to be humbled before God.
17:
The catalogue of rebellion deepens, and the witnesses set the people's refusal against God's readiness to pardon. The reformed John Gill reads "refused to obey" of sheer obstinacy — though exhorted, admonished, and threatened, they would not hear. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather the whole charge: they refused to obey, were not mindful of the wonders God had done among them, hardened their necks, and appointed a captain to return to their bondage; yet against all this stands the great confession that God is a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsook them not.

Over the clause "in their rebellion appointed a captain" the witnesses turn text-critics. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke judges the Hebrew "in their rebellion" a probable error for "in Egypt," a reading found in seven of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts, in the Septuagint, and in the parallel of Numbers 14:4, so that the clause should run, "they appointed a captain to return to their bondage in Egypt." Charles Ellicott concurs, preferring "in Egypt" on the same manuscript and Septuagint authority, and noting that the phrase "a God ready to pardon" is literally "a God of pardons," an expression found only here, at Daniel 9:9, and at Psalms 130:4. A further question runs beneath the words: whether the fathers actually set up a captain or only proposed one. John Wesley reads "made" as "designed and resolved" to do so, for in Numbers 14:4 the appointment was but intended; and as Abraham is said to have offered up Isaac in Hebrews 11:17 because he meant to do it, so Israel is said to have done what they had resolved. Ellicott notes the same, that in the earlier passage the appointment is only proposed.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the two great sins the verse compresses: the meditated return to Egyptian slavery, which for the sake of the garlic and the onions they preferred to the glorious liberty of God's Israel, in distrust of his power and contempt of his promise; and, in the verse following, the Egyptian idolatry of the calf. Yet over the whole ingratitude Henry sets the wonder of the pardon: they found him a God ready to pardon, a God of pardons, who had proclaimed his name as forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin, after Exodus 34:6; though they forsook him, he forsook not them. The witnesses do not divide on the mercy, and only weigh the words — whether the bondage they turned back toward was named as rebellion or as Egypt, and whether the captain was raised or only resolved — while all agree that the God against whom they rebelled is the God of pardons who would not let them go.
18:
The confession names the worst provocation of the wilderness, the golden calf, and the witnesses measure both the folly and the mercy that followed it. The reformed John Gill fixes the origin of the idol: they made them a molten calf in imitation of the Apis, the sacred ox of the Egyptians, carrying the very superstition of their house of bondage into the camp of the redeemed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the emphatic force of the sentence — "yea, they even made them a molten calf" — and the double outrage that they said of it, "This is thy God that brought thee up out of Egypt," ascribing to a cast image the deliverance that was God's alone, and so wrought great provocations; the closing phrase, they note, is a kind of refrain that the prayer sounds again.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry calls it plainly the second of their two great sins: after meditating a return to Egyptian slavery, they fell into Egyptian idolatry, making a molten calf and being so sottish as to say, "This is thy God." The very absurdity of it is part of the charge — that a people so lately carried through the sea on dry land should bow to a thing of melted earrings and credit it with their rescue. It was, in the language of the psalm that laments this apostasy, to change their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass, as Psalms 106:20 mourns.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers up the wilderness rebellion into one shameful image. What makes the calf so grievous is not merely that it broke the first commandment, but that it did so at the foot of the mountain where that commandment had just been spoken, and that it robbed the true Deliverer of his glory to give it to an idol borrowed from Egypt. Gill fixes the Egyptian pattern, Keil and Delitzsch the emphatic "yea" and the blasphemous ascription, and Henry the sottishness of a redeemed people worshipping a calf. And yet the prayer sets this darkest sin exactly where the light will break, for the next words are not of wrath but of mercy: the same God who was robbed of his honour did not, in his manifold compassion, forsake them in the wilderness. The confession names the calf not to despair but to magnify the pardon; the worse the provocation, the more astonishing the grace that bore with it — a pattern the whole chapter, and the whole history of Israel, will trace again and again.
19:
Against the golden calf the prayer sets the marvel of a mercy that would not withdraw, and the witnesses dwell on the pillar that stayed. The reformed John Gill reads "yet thou in thy manifold mercies forsookest them not in the wilderness" with an eye to the desert's peril: God did not cast them off where no supply could be had, where to be forsaken was to be lost. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the confession forward through the continued gifts — the pillar of cloud that departed not by day to lead them, the pillar of fire that failed not by night to show them light, and, in the verses following, the good Spirit, the manna, and the water — all set down as tokens of a grace that outlasted their sin. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the Hebrew of "the pillar of the cloud departed not from them," which is literally "from over them," and recalls again the three offices of that one miraculous cloud — going before to guide, burning by night to give light, and hovering over the camp to refresh and to shade.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds here the very heart of the confession's logic. The Levites mention the pillar again, he observes, on purpose to magnify the mercy: though the people had by their sins provoked God to withdraw from them and leave them to wander and perish in the by-paths of the wilderness, yet in his manifold mercy he continued to lead them and took not away the pillar of cloud and fire, as the earlier verse had recorded at Nehemiah 9:12. When mercies, though forfeited, are still continued, Henry urges, we are bound to be doubly thankful — for the pillar that stood over the camp of the calf-makers was grace upon grace, mercy where wrath was deserved.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse becomes the confession's turning-word, the great "yet" that answers the "but" of their rebellion. They dealt proudly, they made the calf; yet God forsook them not. Gill fixes the peril of the place, where forsaking would have been death; Keil and Delitzsch the string of continued gifts; Clarke the sheltering cloud in its threefold service; and Henry the double thankfulness owed for mercies that sin had forfeited and grace restored. For the congregation now confessing, the point is more than historical. If God did not take away the pillar from a people who had just crowned a calf, then the seed of those people, however unworthy, may still hope in a mercy that is manifold — a compassion measured not by their deserving but by his own great heart, which will not forsake the work of his hands even in the wilderness of their sin.
20:
Among the mercies of the wilderness the prayer names an inward gift beside the outward, the good Spirit given to teach, and the witnesses find it a remarkable word. The reformed John Gill reads "thou gavest also thy good spirit to instruct them" of the knowledge of the laws delivered to them, taking it, with some, of the spirit of prophecy, and, with Aben Ezra, of the spirit put upon the seventy elders in Numbers 11:17. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the same reference to the elders on whom the Spirit rested in Numbers 11:25, notes that the epithet "good" is given to the Spirit in Psalms 143:10, and observes that the Spirit's teaching function appears here only in the Old Testament — a striking anticipation, he says, of the New Testament, where the Spirit is the great instructor of the people of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the gift beside the law and the sabbath as part of one provision. With the law and the sabbath, he says, God gave his good Spirit to instruct them; and besides the law given on Mount Sinai, the five books of Moses, written as he was moved by the Holy Ghost, were constant instructions to them. Henry points to the visible tokens of that same Spirit in the wilderness generation — Bezaleel filled with the Spirit of God for the work of the tabernacle in Exodus 31:3, Joshua a man in whom the Spirit was in Numbers 27:18, and Caleb who followed the Lord with another spirit in Numbers 14:24 — so that the teaching Spirit was no bare abstraction but a real and manifest grace.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse holds together three provisions in one breath: the Spirit to instruct, the manna not withheld from their mouth, and the water given for their thirst. Bread for the body, water for the throat, and the Spirit for the mind and heart — God supplied every want of a wandering people, the inward as fully as the outward. Gill and Ellicott fix the teaching Spirit in the elders and prophets, Ellicott marking how rare and forward-looking the thought is; Henry spreads it over the whole instruction of Israel by the law, the books of Moses, and the men whom the Spirit filled. For the confessing congregation, the mercy cuts deep: they were not left to grope, but taught; not only fed and watered, but enlightened by God's good Spirit — and their sin was therefore the more inexcusable, that they rebelled against a God who had not withheld even his Spirit from their instruction.
21:
The forty years are gathered into a single astonishing sentence, and the witnesses linger over its every clause. The reformed John Gill reads "forty years didst thou sustain them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing" of a people wanting neither for food nor for raiment, since the verse goes on to name the very garments that did not fail. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes on the marvel of the clothing that "waxed not old," pointing to the great parallel in Deuteronomy 8:4, where Moses reminds Israel that their raiment waxed not old upon them, nor did their foot swell, these forty years. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the whole in the frame of the recited favours — sustained forty years, lacking nothing, their clothes not worn out and their feet not swollen — as the summation of all the wilderness mercies before the prayer turns to the conquest.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marvels at the length and tenderness of the care. Never was a people so long nursed, and so tenderly; forty years God sustained them, and in all that time their clothes waxed not old, and, though the way was rough and tedious, their feet swelled not — for they were carried, he says, as upon eagles' wings, borrowing the figure of Deuteronomy 32:11, where God bears his people as the eagle bears her young. The wilderness that should have destroyed them became, under such keeping, the very scene of their preservation.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse stands as the seal of the whole wilderness recital. Forty years is a long trial, and the trial was severe — a barren waste, a rebellious people, a road with no end in sight for a generation — yet through it all God sustained them so completely that they lacked nothing, down to the clothes on their backs and the feet that bore them. Gill fixes the sufficiency of food and raiment, Clarke the unfailing garments of Deuteronomy 8:4, Keil and Delitzsch the summation of the desert mercies, and Henry the eagle's wing that carried a people who could not carry themselves. For the confessing congregation, the memory presses a double truth: that God is able to keep his own through the longest and hardest wandering, wanting for nothing that they truly need; and that a people so kept, who yet rebelled, had no excuse at all, but stand doubly ashamed before a patience that spread their table and mended their clothes for forty years.
22:
The prayer crosses from the wilderness into the conquest, and the witnesses attend to the kingdoms given and a knot in the wording. The reformed John Gill reads "thou gavest them kingdoms and nations" of the two kingdoms of Sihon and Og and the seven nations of Canaan, the first-fruits of the inheritance. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the verse in its recital — God gave them kingdoms and nations and divided them by boundaries, so that they took possession of the land of Sihon, the land of the king of Heshbon, and the land of Og king of Bashan — the trans-Jordan conquests taken as the earnest of all that should follow. Charles Ellicott agrees that Bashan and the realm of Sihon were seized as the earnest of the possession of Canaan, and notes a double reference to the one Sihon, king of Heshbon.

That doubling the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses as a textual difficulty, for Sihon was himself king of Heshbon, and it is strange to read that they possessed "the land of Sihon, and the land of the king of Heshbon," as though of two men. The words "the land of the king of Heshbon" are wanting in some of De Rossi's manuscripts and in the Septuagint, and Clarke would read simply "the land of Sihon, king of Heshbon," or take the connecting particle as "even" — the land of Sihon, even the land of the king of Heshbon — so that one land and one king are meant, not two. Over the phrase "didst divide them into corners" the witnesses part. John Wesley reads it of the heathen nations, whom God in great measure destroyed and whose remnants he dispersed into corners, cooped up in one town or another while Israel dwelt in a large place; the grammatical-historical Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch rather read it of the land, that God divided these territories unto Israel by their boundaries.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance — that God gave his people the kingdoms of Sihon and Og and the nations of Canaan — but only over two points of reading: whether the second clause names a second king or repeats the one Sihon of Heshbon, as Clarke and Ellicott hold; and whether the "corners" are the cramped remnants of the driven-out heathen, as Wesley takes it, or the boundaries by which the land was portioned to the tribes, as the grammatical-historical witnesses prefer. What none of them doubts is the mercy the verse records: the same God who led them forty years through the waste now put whole kingdoms into their hands, making good, in Sihon and Og and the seven nations, the land he had sworn to Abraham to give.
23:
The promise to the patriarch flowers into a nation, and the witnesses hear the old oath fulfilled. The reformed John Gill reads "their children also multipliedst thou as the stars of heaven" as the express fulfilment of the promise once made to Abraham; for their number, when they came out of Egypt and stood on the border of Canaan, was upward of six hundred thousand men, besides women and children — a people grown, from one man, into a multitude none could count. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the confession on: God multiplied their children as the stars of heaven and brought them into the land concerning which he had promised their fathers that they should go in to possess it — the increase and the entrance set side by side, the swelling of the seed and the gift of the soil, as two halves of one kept word.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the mercy briefly but pointedly: God made them so numerous as to replenish the land, and so victorious as to be masters of it. The multiplying was itself a marvel of grace — that a company which went down into Egypt as seventy souls should come up as a nation like the stars for multitude, exactly as God had shown Abraham the heavens and bidden him number them if he could, in Genesis 15:5, and had sworn to multiply his seed as the stars in Genesis 22:17.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse binds the whole recital together, from the call of the one man to the settling of his countless seed. What God had promised Abraham under the night sky he made good in the census of the plains of Moab; and what he had sworn concerning the land he made good in bringing that multitude into it. Gill fixes the number that answered the oath, and Keil and Delitzsch the joining of the increase to the entrance, both grounded in the word given to the fathers. Moses himself had marvelled that the Lord had made them, from a few, as the stars of heaven for multitude, in Deuteronomy 10:22. For the confessing congregation — a remnant lately returned, few and straitened and afraid — the memory carries a quiet plea: the God who once turned one wandering man into a nation like the stars, and brought that nation into the promised land, is not exhausted of the power that keeps his oath; and the seed that had been so multiplied, though now thinned by exile, is still the seed of the promise he made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
24:
The children enter where the fathers could not, and the witnesses mark both the fulfilment and its subjects. The reformed John Gill dwells on the very wording — "so the children went in and possessed the land" — and finds in it the reason for the phrase: not the fathers who came out of Egypt, for they died in the wilderness, all excepting two, but their children, who inherited the promise their parents had forfeited by unbelief, as the sentence upon that generation is recorded in Numbers 14:29. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the recital through the conquest: the children went in and possessed the land, and God subdued before them the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, and gave them into their hands with their kings and the people of the land, that they might do with them as they would — the whole country and its rulers delivered up to a people who had done nothing to earn it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the victory as pure gift. God made them so victorious as to be masters of the land; the natives were given into their hands, that they might do with them as they pleased, and set their feet, if they would, upon the necks of their kings — as Joshua's captains once set their feet upon the necks of the conquered kings in Joshua 10:24. The conquest was not the achievement of Israel's sword but the surrender granted by Israel's God, who subdued the inhabitants before them.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse quietly teaches two things at once. First, that the fathers' unbelief cost them the very land they were brought out to inherit, so that a whole generation fell in the desert while their children entered — a sobering witness, in the midst of a confession of sin, that God's promises are sure but that unbelief may shut a man out of his own portion. And second, that the entrance, when it came, was all of grace: the children did not so much take the land as receive it, for God subdued the Canaanites before them and gave kings and peoples into their hand. Gill fixes the passing of the promise from the faithless fathers to the entering children, Keil and Delitzsch the delivering up of the land and its kings, and Henry the mastery that was God's gift and not Israel's feat. For the confessing congregation, the double lesson is their own: that sin can forfeit an inheritance, and that only sovereign mercy can bestow one.
25:
The recital of grace rises to its height in a land already furnished, and the witnesses note both the plenty and its peril. The reformed John Gill reads "they took strong cities" of fortresses so mighty they were said, in an old hyperbole, to be walled up to heaven, as the spies reported in Deuteronomy 1:28; and he marks the abundance that followed — a fat land, houses full of all good things, wells digged, vineyards and oliveyards and fruit trees in plenty, all found ready to their hand. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the catalogue in the frame of the recital: they took strong cities and a fat land, possessed houses full of all goods, and so did eat and were filled and became fat and delighted themselves in God's great goodness — the summit of the mercies, from which the next verse will mark the fall.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads a warning into that very fatness. They "became fat, and delighted themselves," he says — that is, they grew effeminate, fell under the power of luxury, got wholly corrupted in their manners, sinned against all the mercies of God, and then were destroyed by his judgments. He points the moral with an old saying, that war begets poverty, poverty peace, peace affluence, affluence luxury and corruption of manners, and hence fresh broils and desolations; and he cites a Roman historian to the same effect, that an empire easily held by the arts that won it is lost when idleness supplants labour and pride and appetite drive out self-command.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse becomes a hinge between mercy and rebellion. What God gave was overwhelming — cities they did not build, houses they did not fill, wells they did not dig, vineyards and olives they did not plant — the whole comfort of a settled and prosperous life laid ready in their hands. Gill fixes the plenty, Keil and Delitzsch the delight in God's great goodness, and Clarke the danger folded within the delight. For the fatness that was meant to feed thankfulness fed self-indulgence instead, exactly as Moses had feared when he warned that a full people might forget the God who fed them, and as the song foretold that Jeshurun, waxen fat, would kick, in Deuteronomy 32:15. The confessing congregation names the abundance not to boast in it but to see where it led — that the good land, richly given, became the scene of the ingratitude the very next verse will lament.
26:
In the good land the old rebellion breaks out afresh, and the witnesses read the sharpest ingratitude of the whole confession. The reformed John Gill marks the plain word "nevertheless" — that after all these favours and mercies they were disobedient and rebelled against God, which he calls great ingratitude, the returning of injury for kindness. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as a general condemnation of Israel's whole conduct from the entrance into Canaan to the captivity, then justified by the facts that follow. In proof of their rebellion they cast God's commandments behind their back, an image from 1 Kings 14:9 and Ezekiel 23:35, and they slew the prophets who testified against them to turn them back — Zechariah, stoned in the temple court in 2 Chronicles 24:21, and the prophets cut down in the days of Jezebel, of whom Elijah complained in 1 Kings 19:10; the testifying against sinners, they note, is the language of 2 Kings 17:13, and the closing clause is the same refrain of "great provocations" sounded before.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the horror of it. Though they delighted themselves in God's great goodness, that would not hold them to him; nevertheless they were disobedient and wrought great provocations. Chief among these, they abused God's prophets and slew them, because those prophets testified against them to turn them to God — so returning the greatest injury for the greatest kindness. For the prophets were God's mercy in living form, sent to reclaim a straying people; and to murder the messenger of reclamation was to spurn the very hand stretched out to save.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers the long apostasy of the settled nation into two acts: they flung the law behind them, and they killed the men God sent to call them back. Gill fixes the ingratitude, Keil and Delitzsch the cast-off commandments and the martyred prophets, and Henry the monstrous exchange of injury for kindness. It is the sin the Lord himself would one day lay to Jerusalem's charge, that she killed the prophets and stoned them that were sent unto her, in Matthew 23:37. For the confessing congregation, the memory is a mirror held to their own house: the God against whom their fathers rebelled had not left them to their rebellion, but sent prophet after prophet in patient mercy — and the measure of the nation's guilt was the measure of that spurned kindness, a law thrown down and a long succession of God's servants slain.
27:
The prayer turns to the pattern of the judges — sin, servitude, cry, and rescue — and the witnesses trace the rhythm of mercy. The reformed John Gill reads "thou deliveredst them into the hand of their enemies, who vexed them" of the successive oppressors of that age, the kings of Mesopotamia, Moab, Canaan, and the rest, into whose power God gave a rebellious people. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch refer the whole verse to the times of the judges, after Judges 2:11, and identify the "saviours" whom God raised up as the judges themselves, who delivered Israel out of the hand of their oppressors, as at Judges 3:9; the phrase "many times," they note, marks how often the cycle turned.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sums the era in a sentence: the whole book of Judges is a history of God's mercies and their rebellions — a record, that is, of grace answering fresh apostasy, deliverance following renewed sin, over and over. Charles Ellicott confirms that the very phraseology of this verse and the next shows how carefully the Book of Judges is remembered in the prayer, the Levites reaching back to that history for the words of their confession.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the mercy of it. When they had by their provocations sold themselves into the hands of their enemies, then upon their submission and humble request God gave them saviours — the judges, by whom he wrought many a great deliverance for them when they were on the very brink of ruin. And this, Henry insists, was not for any merit of theirs, for they deserved nothing but ill, but according to his mercies, his manifold mercies. The witnesses do not divide, and together they lay bare the strange grace of the judges' age. God heard from heaven the cry of a people who had earned only wrath, and raised up deliverer after deliverer to save them out of troubles their own sin had brought — Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon, and the rest, each a fresh proof that the LORD is slow to give his people over to the ruin they court. For the confessing congregation, the pattern is precious beyond history: it shows a God who answers the cry of the guilty, who counts a humble request enough to move his compassion, and who, when his people turn to him in their distress, is found again and again a Saviour. The very rhythm of relapse and rescue becomes an argument for hope, that a people once more in trouble may once more cry, and once more be heard.
28:
The cycle turns again, and the witnesses watch a people who could learn from neither judgment nor deliverance. The reformed John Gill reads "but after they had rest" of the seasons when, saved from their enemies, they enjoyed their liberty and their prosperity — and in that very ease did evil again before God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the whole revolving pattern: after they had rest they did evil again, so that God left them once more in the hand of their enemies to have dominion over them; yet when they returned and cried to him, he heard them from heaven and many times delivered them according to his mercies. The rest bred forgetfulness, the forgetfulness bred sin, the sin brought back the oppressor, and the oppression drove them again to their knees — and each time the mercy met the cry.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fastens on the melancholy heart of it. After they had rest, they did evil again; they were not wrought upon either by their troubles or by their deliverances out of trouble. Neither the rod nor the rescue would hold them to their duty; neither fear nor love could keep them. This, Henry sees, is the deepest indictment of the era — not merely that they sinned, but that nothing cured them: the affliction that should have humbled and the salvation that should have won them alike ran off a heart bent on backsliding, so that the same story had to be told again and again through the whole book of the judges, as at Judges 3:12 and Judges 4:1.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse presses a searching truth upon every reader. Here is human nature laid bare: a people delivered who forget their Deliverer the moment the pressure lifts, whom prosperity makes proud and safety makes careless, and who must be driven back to God by fresh distress because they will not be drawn by kindness. Gill fixes the ease that bred the evil, Keil and Delitzsch the whole turning wheel of sin and rescue, and Henry the terrible constancy of a heart that neither trouble nor mercy could change. And yet the verse is not without its comfort, for the same God who left them to their enemies still heard them when they returned, and many times delivered them according to his mercies. The confessing congregation, owning that they too are of this stock, plead that the mercy which so often met the cry of a relapsing people may meet their cry once more.
29:
The prayer passes to the age of the kings, and the witnesses hear God testifying and Israel resisting. The reformed John Gill reads "thou testifiedst against them" of God's sending prophets to admonish the people of their sins and remind them of their duty — the standing witness of heaven against a straying nation. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch expound the clause "which if a man do, he shall live in them," drawn from the great promise of Leviticus 18:5 and echoed in Ezekiel 20:11: the law God testified was no burden but the way of life, and yet they would not walk in it. For "they gave a resisting shoulder," Keil and Delitzsch point to Zechariah 7:11 and find the figure taken from the ox that rears against the yoke and will not bear it, as in Hosea 4:16 — a backsliding heifer that shrinks from the harness.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the tragedy of the withdrawing shoulder. God testified against them, he says, that he might bring them again to his law, to lay their necks under its yoke and walk by its rule; and though they were told how much it would be for their own advantage to keep his judgments, since if a man do them he shall live in them, yet they would not do them, and so in effect said they would not live. They forsook their own mercies. Henry marks that this abridgment of the covenant — do this and live — is taken up in Galatians 3:12 to show that the law is not of faith; and he presses the sad image of the margin, that they gave a withdrawing shoulder, pretending to lay it under the burden of God's law but soon flying off, refusing to abide by it, shrinking back when it came to the setting-to.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse lays bare the perversity of a people who would not be saved on the kindest terms. God did not merely command; he testified, warned, and pleaded, holding out life itself as the reward of obedience. Gill fixes the prophets sent to admonish, Keil and Delitzsch the law that was the way of life and the shoulder that reared against it like an unbroken ox, and Henry the folly of men who forsook their own mercies and, refusing to do what would have made them live, chose in effect to die. It is the same pride that hardened the neck at Sinai, now grown into the settled obstinacy of the kingdom years; and the confessing congregation owns it as the sin of their own fathers, a resisting shoulder set against a yoke that was nothing but their good.
30:
The confession dwells on the long patience of God with a nation past mending, and the witnesses measure the years and the Spirit. The reformed John Gill reads "yet many years didst thou forbear them" of God's longsuffering throughout the reigns of many kings; and he notes the marginal sense, "thou didst draw upon them," which the older interpreters took, with Jarchi, of God drawing out his mercy from his very heart and prolonging it toward them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that same drawing-out as the extending of favour for a long time, comparing the language of Jeremiah 31:3, and reckon the patience to have run the whole span of the kingly rule from Solomon to the Assyrians; the giving of the people at last into the hand of the peoples of the lands, they observe, after Psalms 106:41, began with the Assyrian invasion that destroyed the northern kingdom.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supposes the verse to look chiefly to the ten tribes, and reckons the forbearance at some two hundred and fifty-four years, from their separation from the house of David to their captivity under Shalmaneser; through the whole of which time God warned them by his prophets, or, as the text says, by his Spirit in his prophets — a phrase, Clarke adds, that gives the true notion of divine inspiration, for God's Spirit was given to the prophets, and they testified to the people as they were taught and moved by that Spirit.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the mercy and the means. Many years God forbore them, as loath to punish and waiting to see whether they would repent; and he testified against them by his Spirit in his prophets. That testimony, Henry insists, was the testimony of the Spirit in the prophets, and it was the Spirit of Christ in them, after 1 Peter 1:11; they spoke as they were moved by the Holy Ghost, and what they said is to be received accordingly. God sends prophets, Henry adds, in compassion to his people, as the Chronicler says at 2 Chronicles 36:15, that he may not send judgments; he stretched out his hands, but no man regarded, and only then gave them up. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch fix the long-drawn mercy and its Assyrian end, Clarke the centuries of warning to the ten tribes and the doctrine of inspiration folded into the phrase, and Henry the Spirit of Christ pleading through the prophets with a people who would not hear — so that the captivity, when it came, fell only after generations of a patience they had wearied out.
31:
Even the judgment is bounded by mercy, and the witnesses rest on the God who would not make an end. The reformed John Gill reads "nevertheless for thy great mercies' sake" of the displaying and magnifying of that mercy which is so large and exceeding abundant — the very greatness of the divine compassion being the reason a guilty people was not consumed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch ground the sparing in God's own promise: in the midst of these judgments he did not, according to his word in Jeremiah 4:27 and Jeremiah 30:11, utterly forsake his people or make a full end of them, but suffered them not to become extinct in exile, preserving a remnant and delivering it from captivity. The captivity was real and deserved, but it was not annihilation; a seed was kept.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the two halves of the mercy. When God did punish them, he did not utterly consume them nor forsake them; had he forsaken them, they would have been utterly consumed, but he did not stir up all his wrath, for he designed their reformation and not their destruction. Here is the restraint of a Father's anger — a chastening meant to correct, not to kill; a wrath held deliberately short of what sin deserved, precisely so that a people might be brought back and not blotted out.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse becomes the resting-place of the whole long confession of sin. After the calf and the murdered prophets, the withdrawing shoulder and the wearied patience, the story might have ended in a full end; and it did not, only because God is a gracious and merciful God. Gill fixes the greatness of the mercy that spared them, Keil and Delitzsch the promise that kept a remnant alive through the exile, and Henry the wrath restrained for the sake of reformation. The congregation confessing these things are themselves the living proof of the verse, for they are that preserved remnant, come back from the captivity that might have swallowed them whole. That God did not consume them is the very reason there is a people left to pray; and the same mercy which kept the seed through the fire of judgment is the mercy they now plead, that a God who would not make a full end of their fathers will not make an end of them.
32:
The long recital becomes at last a petition, and the witnesses gather round the one request of the whole prayer. The reformed John Gill notes that the great titles here heaped upon God — the great, the mighty, and the terrible God, who keepeth covenant and mercy — are the very titles Nehemiah gives elsewhere, which makes it likely, he thinks, that the whole prayer is Nehemiah's own composure, delivered by him to the Levites. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the plea plainly: may God, who keepeth covenant and mercy, now also look upon the affliction of his people — though kings, rulers, priests, and people have fully deserved this punishment — for they are bondmen still, and in great affliction, in the land of their fathers. Charles Ellicott marks that here the prayer proper begins, and names the "kings of Assyria" the rod of God's anger, after Isaiah 10:5, tracing through the sacred record the successive scourges — Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sargon, Sennacherib, Esarhaddon.

The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh the words. Adam Clarke reads in the roll of sufferers — kings, princes, priests, prophets, fathers, and all the people — the whole frame of civil and sacred society, from the supreme power down to the common man, all sharing in the trouble. John Wesley marks why the prayer adds "mercy" to "covenant": because the covenant in itself was no sufficient ground of hope, since they had so basely broken it that God was discharged from keeping it; and therefore they fly to his free and rich mercy for relief.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the modesty and the ground of the request. This is the only petition in all the long prayer — that the trouble might not seem little before God — and the trouble was universal, fallen upon kings, princes, priests, prophets, fathers, and all the people, of long continuance, from the time of the kings of Assyria to that day. They do not prescribe to God what he shall do, Henry observes, but leave it to him, desiring only that he would take cognizance of it, remembering that when he saw the affliction of his people in Egypt to be great he came down to deliver them, in Exodus 3:7. In the request they have an eye to God as one to be feared, for he is the great, the mighty, and the terrible God, as Moses names him in Deuteronomy 7:21, and as one to be trusted, for he keeps covenant and mercy, as Daniel confesses in Daniel 9:4.
