The witnesses do not divide: they leave the people casting a universal and long-borne affliction upon a God whose greatness they revere and whose covenant-mercy they plead.
33:
Before they ask relief the people justify their Judge, and the witnesses honour the confession of God's righteousness. The reformed John Gill reads "thou art just in all that is brought upon us" of a people owning the rightness of God's dealings — they could complain of no wrong, and had he shown them no mercy at all, it would have been but what they deserved. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the ground of the confession: God is just concerning all that has befallen them, because their sins deserved the punishment, and he has only fulfilled his word upon the sinners; the acknowledgment stands with the same word of righteousness owned at Nehemiah 9:8, and echoes the confessions of Deuteronomy 32:4 and Ezra 9:15. They note, too, that in the verse following the prophets are omitted from the roll of the guilty, since as God's witnesses they are not reckoned among the transgressors, though they shared in the common suffering.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the abiding lesson. It becomes us, he says, when we are under the rebukes of providence, be they ever so sharp or ever so long continued, still to justify God, and to own that we are punished less than our iniquities deserve. The confession of God's justice is not a formality but the very posture of true penitence, which lays the whole blame where it belongs.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the acknowledgment beside the petition as its necessary companion. The trouble was less, they own, than they had deserved; they justify God in all their troubles, that he had done them no wrong. "We have done wickedly in breaking thy laws," they say in effect, "and therefore thou hast done right in bringing all these miseries upon us." It becomes us, Henry urges, when we are under the rebukes of divine providence, however sharp and however long, to justify God and to judge ourselves, for he will be clear when he judgeth, as David owns in Psalms 51:4. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the desert that would have warranted even unmixed judgment, Keil and Delitzsch the righteousness of a God who does but keep his word upon sinners, and Wesley and Henry the penitent's duty to clear God and condemn himself. It is the very sinew of the confession: only a people who own that God is just in all he has brought upon them can plead, without presumption, for the mercy they do not deserve.
34:
The confession names every order of the nation as guilty, and the witnesses mark the sweep of it and one telling omission. The reformed John Gill reads the roll — our kings, our princes, our priests, nor our fathers — as taking in all ranks of men, from the highest to the lowest, who had shown no regard nor yielded any obedience to the holy law of God. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the subject is again emphatically marked, and that in this enumeration of the classes of the people the prophets are deliberately left out, because, as God's witnesses, they are not to be reckoned among the transgressors, though they were involved in the sufferings that fell on the nation.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the same omission and its reason. In this verse, he observes, the confession acknowledges that the kings, the princes, the priests, and the fathers had broken the law — but the prophets are left out, for they continued faithful to God, testifying by his Spirit against the crimes of all, and this even at the risk of their lives. Charles Ellicott simply underscores the point: note that the prophets are omitted in this enumeration.

The witnesses do not divide, and together they draw out the significance of who is named and who is not. The guilt is national and total — the throne, the nobility, the priesthood, and the mass of the fathers all stand charged with breaking the law and refusing the commandments and testimonies wherewith God testified against them. Gill fixes the reach of the indictment from top to bottom, and Keil and Delitzsch, Clarke, and Ellicott together fix the honourable exception. That the prophets alone are spared the charge is no small thing in a confession like this: it marks them as the one faithful order in a faithless nation, the men who bore God's witness against kings and priests and people, and who suffered with the guilty though they were not of them. The lesson for the confessing congregation is sobering and clear. Their rulers and priests and fathers had failed them and God together; only the prophets, speaking by the Spirit, had kept faith — and those very prophets their fathers had too often slain. To confess the sin of every order and to honour the fidelity of the prophets is to own both how wide the corruption ran and how graciously God had never left himself without a witness.
35:
The confession sharpens to a particular charge: even in their own kingdom and their own good land they would not serve God. The reformed John Gill reads "they have not served thee in their kingdom" of the whole history of the state, whether of Israel or of Judah, and even in their most flourishing circumstances — the times of greatest plenty being no better than the times of want in point of obedience. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take "in their kingdom" of the independent kingdom God had given them, and "in thy great goodness" of the fulness of blessing in the midst of which they lived; the "large and fat land," they add, is the wide land of Exodus 3:8, and still they turned not from their wicked works.

Over the reading of the phrase the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke offers a variant. Instead of "in their kingdom," he notes, two of Kennicott's manuscripts, together with the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic, read "in thy kingdom" — a reading he judges most likely to be the true one, so that the charge becomes that they did not serve God in the very kingdom that was his. Where the grammatical-historical witnesses keep the received "their kingdom," meaning the realm God bestowed, Clarke would have it "thy kingdom," pressing that all their dominion was in truth the LORD's.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the sin to its double point. This is a contempt of the good land God had given them: "our kings have not served thee in their kingdom," not used their power for the support of religion; and "our people have not served thee" in the use of the gifts of God's great goodness, in that large and fat land which he not only gave them by grant but gave before them by the expulsion of the natives. Those who would not serve God in their own land, Henry observes, were made to serve their enemies in a strange land, exactly as Moses had threatened in Deuteronomy 28:47; for it is a pity a good land should have bad inhabitants, and fatness and fulness often make men proud and sensual, as the song warned of Jeshurun in Deuteronomy 32:15. The witnesses do not divide over the substance — that a people richly blessed and freely settled refused the service they owed — and part only over a word, whether the kingdom is called theirs or God's; a difference that, either way, deepens the charge, since the realm they would not serve God in was the realm his own hand had given.
36:
The confession comes at last to the bitter present, and the witnesses feel the weight of "servants this day." The reformed John Gill reads it exactly: though they had leave to return to their land and rebuild their city and temple, they were still in subjection to the kings of Persia — free in name, but bondmen in fact, in the very land God gave their fathers. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the two clauses of the plea together: the prayer that God would not lightly regard the trouble of his people is now supported by the state they are in — bondmen in the land which God gave to their fathers as a free people, bondmen of the Persian monarchs, and the increase of the land belonging to the kings who rule over them. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states the political fact plainly: they had no king of their own and were under the government of the kings of Persia, to whom they paid a regular tribute.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the sad reversal in it. Free-born Israelites are enslaved, he says, and the land which they had long held by the most honourable tenure of all — by immediate grant from the crown of heaven, as a peculiar people above all people on the earth — they now hold by as base a tenure as villenage itself, by and from and under the kings of Persia, whose vassals they were. A sad change, Henry exclaims, but see what work sin makes; for poverty and slavery are the fruits of sin, and it is sin that brings us into all our distresses.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers the whole confession to its point. The land was still theirs to till, the city rising again, the temple standing; and yet they were servants in it, its fruit going to a foreign crown, its people the subjects of a distant king. Gill fixes the subjection that outlasted the return, Keil and Delitzsch the bondage in the land of the fathers, and Clarke the tribute of a kingless people; and Henry the tragedy that a nation given the freest of all inheritances had, by sin, sunk to the servitude of vassals. It is the same lesson the whole prayer has taught, that sin forfeits mercy and turns blessing into bondage; and it is the very ground of their appeal, for a people who own themselves servants "this day," and own it justly for their sins, cast themselves upon the mercy of the God who once heard bondmen cry in Egypt, as Ezra too had confessed that in their bondage God had not forsaken them, in Ezra 9:9.
37:
The affliction is spelled out to its last hard detail, and the witnesses reckon what the bondage cost. The reformed John Gill reads "it yieldeth much increase unto the kings" of a land very fruitful, yet fruitful not for its own people but for foreign kings, who exacted much toll, tribute, and custom, so that the profit of the earth was greatly lessened to those who worked it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse as the completion of the plea of the verse before: the increase of the land God gave belongs to the kings set over them because of their sins, who have dominion over their bodies and their cattle at their pleasure, so that they are in great distress. Charles Ellicott adds the historian's detail — that a very large amount in money and in kind was sent from Syria to the Persian treasury — and notes that the dominion over their bodies was for military service, the priests not omitting even themselves from the reckoning.

Over the phrase "in great distress" the witnesses differ a little. The wesleyan-arminian voices read it of the outward oppression: Adam Clarke of a people from whom personal and feudal services were exacted at the ruler's pleasure, so that they could call neither their persons nor their time nor their land nor their cattle their own; and John Wesley of men who plough and sow and labour, and God blesses their endeavours, yet in great measure not for themselves, as formerly, but for their kings, to whom they pay heavy tributes, and who force both them and their beasts to do as they please. Ellicott, by contrast, hears in the distress something deeper than the Persian yoke — a grief not so much at the tribute as at the remembrance of God's judgments, for the whole pathos of the verse lies in the comparison between the divine purpose in first giving the land and their present bondage in it.

The witnesses do not divide over the fact of the misery, only over where its sharpest sting lay — in the exactions of the crown, as Clarke and Wesley feel it, or in the shame of a covenant people reduced, for their sins, to servitude in their own inheritance, as Ellicott discerns. What all agree upon is the completeness of the subjection this verse records: the land's increase drained away to foreign kings, and the very bodies and cattle of the people theirs to command. It is exactly the bondage Moses had foretold, that a nation whose fruit and labour a stranger should eat would be only oppressed and crushed always, as Deuteronomy 28:33 warned; and it is out of this distress, owned as the just wage of sin, that the covenant of the next verse is born.
38:
The long confession issues at last in a bond, and the witnesses read the covenant that closes the day. The reformed John Gill takes "because of all this" of the whole distress just rehearsed — or, with Jarchi and Aben Ezra, "in the midst of all this evil" — so that in the very depth of their affliction, and that it might be removed, they resolve to bind themselves anew to God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it as founded on the confession: on the ground of all they have owned, and to prove their sincerity, they make a sure covenant and write it, and their princes, Levites, and priests seal unto it — each party, he explains, impressing his seal upon moist clay that was afterward hardened, or attaching the seal to the document by a separate string, as the plural form "those on the sealed documents" implies at Nehemiah 11:1. John Wesley marks the permanence of it: the sure covenant was sealed and left upon record, that it might stand a witness against them if ever they dealt deceitfully.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the sealing as the act of a people persuaded that they had brought all their miseries upon themselves by their transgressions, and now devoting themselves to God's service, to do with them as he pleased. He finds in the signatories a picture of the commonwealth as it then stood — a mixed government in which the nobles bore the civil office and the priests and Levites the sacred, each order distinct yet mutually supporting the other, the state not modelling the church nor the church meddling with the state; a balance under which, he says, every public blessing may be looked for, since to Caesar are rendered the things that are Caesar's and to God the things that are God's, after the word of Matthew 22:21.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into its conclusion. After so long a remonstrance of their case, they came at last to this resolution, to return to God and their duty and oblige themselves never to forsake him; and because they had smarted so much for sin, they would now more firmly than ever bind themselves against it. The covenant, Henry notes, was made with serious consideration, being the result of a chain of suitable thoughts; with great solemnity, written and sealed as a memorial for all ages; with joint consent, that they might strengthen one another's hands; and with fixed resolution, a sure covenant reserving no power of revocation. In it was fulfilled the promise that when the Jews returned they should join themselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant, in Jeremiah 50:5, and should subscribe with their hand unto the LORD, in Isaiah 44:5. The witnesses do not divide: they leave the humbled congregation binding itself, in writing and under seal, to the God whose mercies and whose judgments it had spent the day rehearsing.
